title: Study in pairs
hook: Jewish learning is often done in pairs, arguing over a text

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessings all day: short blessings scattered through the ordinary hours. Your line was a hundred blessings. How many of your five did you find, and which one surprised you? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

Two men in the Talmud studied together: Rabbi Yochanan, a great teacher, and Resh Lakish, who, the story says, had once been a bandit before he turned to learning. Then Resh Lakish died, and Rabbi Yochanan was deeply pained. The rabbis tried to help. They sent him a sharp scholar to sit in the empty seat. Every time Rabbi Yochanan said something, the new partner answered: there's a teaching that supports you. Every single time. It should have been a comfort. It wasn't. Today's word is what Rabbi Yochanan had lost.
screen: `RABBI YOCHANAN AND RESH LAKISH.` → `AN EMPTY SEAT.` → `A PARTNER WHO ALWAYS AGREED.`

segments.voice: Here's what Rabbi Yochanan said, in the Talmud's telling. When I said something, Resh Lakish would raise twenty-four objections, and I would give twenty-four answers, and so the matter became clear. You tell me there's a teaching that supports me. Don't I already know I'm right? That's chavruta. The word is Aramaic, close to chaver, a friend or companion, and it means study in a pair. In a traditional study hall, pairs sit across a table, one text open between them, reading aloud and arguing. Not fighting. Arguing toward the text: what does this line mean, why this word, what about the case it doesn't mention? The noise of a room full of pairs is part of the picture. The Talmud reaches for a verse from Proverbs to explain it. The King James has it: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." The rabbis read it of two students who sharpen each other in learning. And the Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers gives advice in two short pieces: make yourself a teacher, and get yourself a companion. The point isn't agreement. A partner who only nods leaves you where you started. A partner who pushes back makes you say why. Look back over this week. It began with walking as prayer, then turned to Jewish ways. Speaking to God in your own words, alone in a field. Kavanah, the heart aimed. Musar, one trait at a time. The count of the Omer. A hundred blessings. And today, the one practice of the week that needs a second person across the table.
screen: `TWENTY-FOUR OBJECTIONS.` · `CHAVRUTA: A PAIR, ONE TEXT.` · `A TEACHER AND A COMPANION.` · `A WEEK OF JEWISH WAYS.` · then, large: `IRON SHARPENETH IRON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: study one line with a partner, starting with the partner you have right now, which is you. Take the line: iron sharpeneth iron. Say it once, slowly. Ask what it means. Then take the other side: when does a friend dull you instead of sharpening you? Then answer back. Let the two voices take turns, without hurrying. If you pray, you can bring the question before God. If you don't, just let the argument breathe. Later today, find someone to try it with for real. The bell holds the time.
Chavruta. Study in a pair: two people, one text, and plenty of questions across the table. Today's word.
Your line: two heads. Today, take one line you care about, from any book, and read it with someone else. Ask them to push back on it once. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: In yeshivas and study halls, and in adult-learning programs, Jews study Talmud and other texts in pairs called chavrutas, reading aloud and questioning each other line by line.

fork.setup: you're Rabbi Yochanan. your new study partner backs up every word you say with a supporting teaching. how do you respond?
options: thank him: it's good to be agreed with.
tell him you miss the objections that made things clear.
fork.reveal: in the Talmud's telling, he says Resh Lakish raised twenty-four objections, and the answers made the matter clear. agreement taught him nothing.

original.note: Aramaic: companionship, a study partnership; close to Hebrew chaver, friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: study in pairs sounds like a homework buddy.
what it means: two people over one text, reading aloud and questioning each other until the meaning comes clear.
what a scholar hears: Rabbi Yochanan's grief for Resh Lakish's twenty-four objections, and the rabbis reading iron sharpening iron as two students sharpening each other.

notes: Bava Metzia 84a: Resh Lakish's earlier life as a bandit, his death, Rabbi Yochanan's distress, Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat sent to study with him ('there is a teaching that supports you'), and the twenty-four objections and answers. The new partner is left unnamed. Paraphrased; confirm. The story goes on to Rabbi Yochanan's own death from grief; the script stops before that.
Chavruta 'close to chaver, friend': confirm the lexical relation is stated acceptably.
Taanit 7a applies Proverbs 27:17 to two scholars sharpening each other in halakha; paraphrased.
Avot 1:6 (Joshua ben Perachiah: make for yourself a rav and acquire for yourself a chaver) paraphrased.
